scenes.tts: A cold virus sits on a light switch. For many hours, it does nothing on its own. A fingertip can still pick it up. Inside your nose, it gets some of your cells to build new copies of it. So what makes something alive? Do bacteria and viruses pass the test?
scenes.visual: virus on a switch plate does nothing; a fingertip block lifts it; it enters a nose cell and copies appear; question: alive?
scenes.narration: A cold virus sits on a light switch. For many hours, it does nothing on its own. A fingertip can still pick it up. Inside your nose, it gets some of your cells to build new copies of it. So what makes something alive? Do bacteria and viruses pass the test?

scenes.tts: Biologists check a list of characteristics. Living things are made of one or more cells. They take in and use energy. The chemical reactions that do this are called metabolism. They grow, respond, and keep their inside conditions steady. They reproduce, and they change over many generations. No single box decides it. A mature red blood cell cannot divide, but it is still a living cell. A crystal gets bigger, but it has no cells and no metabolism.
scenes.visual: seven-item checklist builds line by line; metabolism label; red blood cell example; crystal grows but fails cells and metabolism
scenes.narration: Biologists check a list of characteristics. Living things are made of one or more cells. They take in and use energy. The chemical reactions that do this are called metabolism. They grow, respond, and keep their inside conditions steady. They reproduce, and they change over many generations. No single box decides it. A mature red blood cell cannot divide, but it is still a living cell. A crystal gets bigger, but it has no cells and no metabolism.

scenes.tts: Now test a bacterium. It is a prokaryote: a living thing made of one cell with no nucleus. In a damp place with food, it takes in nutrients and uses energy. It grows. It responds to its surroundings. Then it splits in two, all by itself. It has its own ribosomes, the parts that build proteins. So a bacterium is a living cell.
scenes.visual: blue rod cell with ribosome dots; nutrients arrive, it lengthens, splits in two; ticks appear on the checklist
scenes.narration: Now test a bacterium. It is a prokaryote: a living thing made of one cell with no nucleus. In a damp place with food, it takes in nutrients and uses energy. It grows. It responds to its surroundings. Then it splits in two, all by itself. It has its own ribosomes, the parts that build proteins. So a bacterium is a living cell.

scenes.tts: Now test a virus. A virus is a tiny infectious agent: genetic material inside a protein coat. That coat is called a capsid. A virus is not a cell, and it has no ribosomes of its own. Outside a cell, it does not take in food, use energy, or grow.
scenes.visual: virus with capsid and DNA or RNA labels; crosses appear on cells, energy, grow
scenes.narration: Now test a virus. A virus is a tiny infectious agent: genetic material inside a protein coat. That coat is called a capsid. A virus is not a cell, and it has no ribosomes of its own. Outside a cell, it does not take in food, use energy, or grow.

scenes.tts: A host cell is the living cell that a virus infects. Inside it, the virus's genes get the cell to build new virus parts. The parts come together as new viruses. The cell does the building. The virus has no metabolism of its own.
scenes.visual: virus enters a host cell; its ribosomes build yellow parts; parts assemble into new viruses
scenes.narration: A host cell is the living cell that a virus infects. Inside it, the virus's genes get the cell to build new virus parts. The parts come together as new viruses. The cell does the building. The virus has no metabolism of its own.

scenes.tts: So the S O L classes viruses as nonliving. A virus is not a cell, it has no metabolism of its own, and it is copied only inside a host cell. Most bacteria carry out life processes by themselves when conditions suit them. Scientists still discuss the question. Keep this rule: bacteria are living cells, and viruses are classed as nonliving.
